title: The Wildberries Theory of Russian Defeat
gist: Ukraine has extended deep strikes from oil refineries to Wildberries, Russia's Amazon-equivalent, hitting at least a dozen warehouses in a week and knocking out an estimated 8% of its logistics capacity with ~$400M in physical damage and up to $2B in seller inventory losses. Kovalev's thesis is that Wildberries is a legitimate military target because it functions as the de facto procurement channel for a Russian army whose official logistics never delivered basics—and simultaneously the fastest way to break Putin's domestic bargain that the war would not touch ordinary Russians.

themes.theme: Wildberries as de facto military procurement chain

insights.claim: Wildberries hosted a dedicated catalog category called 'Everything for the SVO' containing more than 200,000 listings including body armor, tactical helmets, and custom drone components such as drop rigs and tail fins tailored to Russian projectile grenades, which was hastily scrubbed from the site only after Ukrainian strikes began.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Consumer e-commerce is now documented war infrastructure, which means retail logistics assets in belligerent states carry military-target risk that insurers and lenders have not priced.
insights.quote: The catalog included more than 200,000 listings, including not just war-themed coffee mugs but also thousands of battlefield items
insights.locator: Look closer, however, and Wildberries makes an astonishingly obvious target

insights.claim: The author's own research found close to 1,000 Wildberries listings meeting a strict definition of military equipment with no plausible civilian use—body armor plates, combat helmets, drone munitions components, drone detectors, and electronic warfare jamming systems—plus another 4,500 dual-use listings whose demand is visibly combat-driven.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Provides the first quantified estimate of consumer-platform militarization, and a replicable method for scoring how much of a war economy runs through civilian marketplaces.
insights.locator: There isn’t a single figure to indicate how much the Russian army depends

insights.claim: A review of 30 Telegram fundraising channels found more than 18,000 posts over two years linking directly to product pages on Wildberries and its competitor Ozon, with some procurement requests specific enough to include an individual military unit's call sign.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Ozon shares the same targeting logic and exposure as Wildberries—an under-appreciated second-order risk for Russian e-commerce equity and debt.
insights.locator: Hundreds of Telegram channels are fundraising for the army

insights.claim: Wildberries listings carry 'tested in the SVO' badges and official Russian certification stamps alongside near-perfect verified-buyer ratings from customers writing that they were ordering 'for the guys in the SVO,' indicating the platform actively encourages the military trade rather than merely tolerating it.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Platform complicity is documented in its own product metadata—a template for how sanctions and targeting bodies can evidence dual-use commerce.
insights.quote: Many listings come with a “tested in the SVO” badge and official Russian certification stamps, meaning that this trade is actively encouraged by the platform.
insights.locator: Many listings come with a “tested in the SVO” badge

insights.claim: Wildberries' customer review system inadvertently functions as a real-time field-testing report from soldiers, giving Russian volunteer procurement a feedback loop that the Defense Ministry's official chain lacks.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Explains why the informal channel outperforms state procurement: consumer-grade iteration speed applied to battlefield kit is a genuine capability, not just a workaround.
insights.quote: a customer review system that functions, inadvertently, as a real-time field-testing report from soldiers
insights.locator: These efforts depend on precisely the kind of consumer logistics infrastructure

insights.claim: Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov said in December 2024 that more than 65 volunteer-built drone and electronic warfare systems had been delivered to the armed forces since that April, alongside more than 100,000 individual products purchased from small civilian manufacturers and design shops.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: The Kremlin has publicly conceded its dependence on civilian procurement, which is precisely the admission that legitimizes the target set.
insights.locator: The Russian government acknowledges this state of affairs

insights.claim: Russia's official logistics system has never reliably supplied its own soldiers with basics such as thermal imagers, generators, or quality tourniquets, a four-year gap that volunteers and crowdfunders filled and that Ukraine can now attack at its aggregation point.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: The attack targets a single point of failure created by state incompetence—centralized fulfillment is the vulnerability that decentralized crowdfunding accidentally built.
insights.locator: That is what makes the warehouse strikes militarily coherent

themes.theme: Quantified economic damage and financial contagion

insights.claim: By July 22, 2026, after only the first few attacks, Ukraine had knocked out an estimated 8 percent of Wildberries' total logistics capacity, with physical warehouse damage alone estimated at around $400 million.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: A concrete baseline for tracking campaign effectiveness—capacity destruction percentage is the metric to watch as strikes continue.
insights.quote: Ukraine had already knocked out an estimated 8 percent of Wildberries’ total logistics capacity
insights.locator: Beyond the military supply chain effect, the damage is real

insights.claim: Sellers' losses from destroyed Wildberries inventory could reach $2 billion, little of which is recoverable because the company added drone and missile attacks to its force majeure clause shortly before the first strikes, absolving the platform of liability for destroyed stock.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Losses fall entirely on Russian small businesses rather than the platform—concentrated, politically visible pain among an entrepreneurial class that had been pro-war.
insights.locator: Sellers’ losses from destroyed inventory could reach another $2 billion

insights.claim: Wildberries' size means the strikes will ripple across the Russian economy, including damage to the banks holding its substantial debt, with the Kremlin reportedly considering support for the company likely involving already-stressed state-controlled banks.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Physical strikes are being converted into credit stress on an already-strained state banking system—a transmission channel from drones to Russian financial stability.
insights.locator: The company’s sheer size will have other ripple effects

themes.theme: Breaking Putin's insulation bargain with Moscow and St. Petersburg

insights.claim: Unlike fuel, which can be rerouted from remote regions to keep Moscow and St. Petersburg supplied while the provinces bear the shortages, warehouse destruction cannot be reshuffled—infrastructure maintaining swift delivery across 11 time zones hits Putin's core urban clientele directly.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: This is the key asymmetry versus refinery strikes: logistics damage is non-reroutable, so it defeats the regime's regional shock-absorption strategy.
insights.quote: Gasoline can be rerouted from remote regions to keep Russia’s two main cities supplied
insights.locator: Unlike with Ukraine’s refinery attacks, Putin has been unable to protect

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone force commander Robert 'Magyar' Brovdi stated the Wildberries strikes were partly psychological operations aimed at disrupting the 'illusion of a comfortable peacetime' that Russians have been permitted to maintain.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Ukraine is explicitly targeting domestic morale and the regime's social contract, not just materiel—expect more consumer-facing infrastructure in the target set.
insights.locator: Ukrainian drone force commander Robert “Magyar” Brovdi has been candid

insights.claim: Wildberries is an app on every Russian's phone, which makes disruption of it a more profound way of bringing the war home to the Russian middle class than the oil refinery attacks that caused nationwide fuel shortages.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Reframes the target hierarchy in economic warfare: daily-use consumer platforms may deliver more political effect per strike than energy infrastructure.
insights.quote: Wildberries, however, is an app on every Russian’s phone, making the war impossible to ignore.
insights.locator: Putin built his domestic bargain with ordinary Russians

insights.claim: Millions of Russians earn part or all of their living as Wildberries sellers, and social media is full of sellers venting grief over incinerated stock while appearing genuinely incapable of connecting their losses to the invasion many of them had cheered on.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Whether this cognitive disconnect breaks determines if economic pain converts into political pressure—the key uncertainty in the whole strategy.
insights.locator: Tens of millions of ordinary Russians depend on Wildberries

insights.claim: The Russian state's response was to have state media simply ignore the strikes and to detain a 19-year-old woman in Krasnodar on July 24 merely for posting video of the aftermath, indicating the regime views information suppression as its primary countermeasure.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Censorship intensity is a proxy for how damaging the regime privately judges the strikes to be.
insights.locator: The Russian state’s response to the attacks was also predictable

themes.theme: Legal framing and the target-legitimacy argument

insights.claim: Under international humanitarian law a civilian object becomes a legitimate target when its function offers a 'definite military advantage,' and Wildberries passes that test in a way that Russia's strikes on Ukrainian apartment blocks, shopping centers, and maternity clinics do not.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: The legality argument shapes whether Western backers restrict deep-strike weapons use—a direct input to Ukraine's targeting freedom.
insights.quote: a civilian object becomes a legitimate target when its function offers a “definite military advantage.”

insights.claim: Russia has spent years striking Nova Poshta, Ukraine's largest private delivery company, destroying terminals and killing at least a dozen employees including three as recently as July 19, 2026, making Kremlin war-crime accusations over Wildberries hypocritical.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Commercial logistics operators on both sides are now standard targets—an operating-risk shift for any delivery or warehousing business in a war zone.
insights.locator: This is not a strange target for the Ukrainian military

insights.claim: At least a dozen Wildberries warehouses were struck in a single week across Moscow region, St. Petersburg, Tver, occupied Simferopol, Krasnodar, Tambov, and Voronezh, with the flagship facility near Moscow producing a smoke plume visible from space.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kovalev
insights.so_what: Demonstrates Ukrainian deep-strike capacity to hit many dispersed targets deep inside Russia in a compressed window—a step change in tempo and reach.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s campaign of deep strikes against oil refineries
